transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from the NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump has announced that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will take over
as White House Chief of Staff on Monday.
Susie Wiles, who currently holds the job, will move to Trump's political operation.
Talks on Wall Street are trading higher at this hour after a major sell-off on Thursday,
and PR's Scott Horsley says investors also got a better-than-expected report on the job
market.
U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs last month, far more than forecasters had expected.
A new report from the Labor Department also shows hiring in August and September was stronger
than initially reported.
The unemployment rate inched down last month, even as more than 400,000 people came off
the sidelines and started looking for work.
Wage gains inched up, although probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
The stable job market means the Federal Reserve can focus its attention on fighting inflation.
The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate next month.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ stock index clawed back some of the ground it lost on Thursday.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Democrats are preparing to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
NPR's Frank Langford reports some political scientists see a broader significance in the
results.
In a survey ahead of the midterms, most political scientists thought it was more likely than
not that at least five of the most prominent Republicans would allege fraud.
That didn't happen.
And President Trump has said he'll accept the results, which were overwhelming.
Dartmouth professor Brendan Nihan is co-director of the survey, Bright Line Watch.
It's a remarkable turning point.
The threat to democracy has been acute.
It wasn't clear whether he'd be able to subvert this election, but the system held.
The White House said Trump was not a threat to democracy but a defender.
In a statement, it said, "President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure
we have free and fair elections."
Frank Langford, NPR News, Washington.
The head of the Justice Department's National Security Division and the top federal prosecutor
in southern Florida have both stepped down.
NPR's Ryan Lucas reports their departures are the latest to hit the Trump DOJ since
Democrats swept this week's midterm elections.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on social media the resignations of both John
Eisenberg and Jason Redding Quinones.
Eisenberg had kept a low profile while serving as the chief of the National Security Division.
Quinones served as the U.S. attorney for the southern district of Florida, a post from
which he oversaw the Justice Department's sprawling and troubled investigation into
a purported grand conspiracy by President Trump's perceived enemies.
The resignations come a day after the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights
Division, Harmeet Dillon, stepped down, meaning the department has now lost three senior Senate-confirmed
officials since the Republican wipeout in the midterms.
This is NPR News.
John J. Rockefeller, who served as West Virginia governor and longtime senator, has died.
Chris Schulz has more.
Rockefeller's 50-year career at every level of public service began in 1964 as a 27-year-old
volunteer in the small community of Emmons.
He made a name for himself in Charleston and especially on Capitol Hill as an early proponent
of reforming and expanding health care for all Americans.
For a 2015 documentary on his life, Rockefeller told West Virginia Public Broadcasting his
early experiences in the state shaped that lifetime commitment.
Rockefeller is being remembered for his service to the people of West Virginia, especially
coal miners, veterans and children.
For NPR News, I'm Chris Schulz in Morgantown, West Virginia.
A rare dinosaur fossil from France is heading to auction and some scientists are worried
about who buys it.
It's the very specimen researchers use to identify the species.
It includes one of the best-preserved skulls ever discovered from the group of dinosaurs.
Researchers worry that if it goes to a private collection, they could lose access to it.
Giant pandas are back on view at the zoo in Atlanta today for the first time in two years.
After both six years old, they arrive from China in September and have been getting used
to their new home.
The pandas are on a 10-year loan from China.
This is NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Trump names Stephen Miller as next White House Chief of Staff, replacing Susie Wiles
Wall Street trades higher after Thursday sell-off; jobs report beats expectations with 165,000 added
Democrats poised to take control of both congressional chambers in January; Trump says he'll accept results
Justice Department National Security Division chief John Eisenberg and Florida U.S. attorney Jason Reding Quiñones resign
Former West Virginia governor and senator John D. Rockefeller IV dies; remembered for health care advocacy
Rare French dinosaur fossil heading to auction, raising concerns among researchers over future access
Giant pandas from China return to view at Atlanta zoo for first time in two years
